near_misses.why_not: A real overlap (raw input parsed again downstream of the boundary check), but already encoded as `'INP-14': ['DSN-45', 'INP-23']` in scripts/craft-review-workflow.js and in maintenance.md, so no new entry.

Both fire on a bare `exec(` (INP-04 `(?<![.\w$])exec(Sync)?\(`, INP-05 `(?<![.\w])exec\(`), but INP-04 asks whether an outside value reaches a started process through a shell, a split command string or without an allow-list, and INP-05 whether a string is evaluated as code: JavaScript exec(cmd) is the first defect, Python exec(src) the second.

INP-07's Limits claim the listen address's default ('the rule reaches the default value the code supplies, which a secure default makes the specific interface'); INP-09's Validator greps only 'a verification, hostname, CSRF or autoescaping switch', options 'named insecure, unsafe, skip-verify, no-verify or disable-ssl' and options whose name 'carries verify, secure, validate, escape, ssl or tls', so a bind-address default never reaches INP-09's question.

For a table, column or sort identifier from a request both ask for the same allow-list, but for a value INP-02 asks whether it is bound rather than spliced while INP-01 asks whether its field rule is checked, and INP-01's Limits keep both ('a value bound for an SQL query still goes through parameterized queries'); a rule-level DEFER_TO would drop INP-01's validation finding on every spliced value.

INP-22 asks whether a form a lenient parser admits but the stated format excludes is acted on unchecked; INP-01 asks whether the field's allow-list rule is checked. Each Limits hands the other its part: INP-01 'the choice of parser, the grammar of structured input ... are outside it', INP-22 'the full range of acceptable values and conformance to business rules, lie outside it'.

INP-01 asks whether any rejecting server-side check exists; INP-13 whether a structured value's parts are read and checked through its parser instead of the raw text, which INP-01's Limits put outside ('the choice of parser').
Absence versus repetition: INP-01 flags a value that reaches use with no rejecting check, INP-14 processing code that repeats a parse or check the boundary already made.
INP-01 checks a parsed field's length or item count before business processing; INP-24 bounds the raw input's size before it is buffered or parsed — different moments, different checks.
INP-01 asks whether a check of the field's rule exists; INP-17 whether a regular-expression check that exists leaves part of the value unmatched.

Both fire on `Handlebars.compile(src, { noEscape: true })`, but INP-05 asks whether a template is built from untrusted input and its Limits put 'the escaping of output for its context' outside it, which is INP-03's question.
A regex that strips script tags fires both (INP-11 trigger 4, INP-13 trigger 1), but INP-13's Limits list 'sanitizing user-authored HTML' among 'separate controls the rule does not reach'.

INP-17 asks only whether a whole-value regex is anchored; INP-13 asks whether the format has a parser that should read it, and its Limits confine the whole-value regex to 'a simple, structured field that has no standard or established parser of its own, unlike a date or a URL'; INP-13's parser fix satisfies INP-17.
Different questions on one line (raw text instead of the format's parser, versus a regex that uses no regex feature); reported under contradictions because INP-15's fix is INP-13's bad shape.
Different questions on one line (a regex that uses no regex feature, versus a whole-value check that leaves part of the value unmatched); reported under contradictions because their fixes conflict.
INP-13 asks whether raw text is handled instead of a parser; INP-22 whether a parser that is used admits forms the stated format excludes.
INP-21 judges the path after a parse fails; INP-22 a parse that succeeds on a form the format excludes.
Both cite JSON's duplicate-name ambiguity, but INP-22 asks about a lenient parser's result used unchecked and INP-23 about a decode after the check or raw input handed to a second parser.
INP-16's Limits: 'matching the entire value and avoiding excessive backtracking are separate requirements on a pattern, and the score measures neither'.
INP-18's Limits: 'how its matching time grows with the input ... are separate questions; the rule covers whether each construct exists in the running engine with the intended meaning'.
INP-19's length check guards a match on a backtracking engine; INP-24's Validator greps whole-stream reads and parser calls, not regular-expression matches.
INP-17 judges the pattern's anchoring, INP-20 the tests that exercise the pattern.

contradictions.sentence_a: That parse takes the place of splitting the raw text on a delimiter, testing it for a substring, including a prefix or suffix, or matching it with a regular expression, whether to read the format or to check one of its parts. (INP-13 Thesis; its bad half is `if strings.HasSuffix(base, "example.com") {`)
contradictions.sentence_b: A regular expression whose pattern is only literal text, anchored at the start of the input, at its end, at both or at neither, with no flag, and that tests equality, a prefix, a suffix or containment, or, unanchored, replaces every occurrence of one fixed string with another, is written with the string type's own operation for that job, taking as its arguments the literal text the pattern matches and, for a replacement, the literal text it inserts, with anchors and escapes removed. (INP-15 Thesis) Applied to a literal check on a URL such as `re.match(r"https://example\.com/", url)`, its fix is `url.startswith("https://example.com/")`, the prefix test on raw URL text INP-13 calls bad.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A literal pattern that reads or checks a part of text in a format with a standard or established parser, such as a URL's scheme or host or a date's fields, is outside the rule: its fix is that parser and a check on the parsed component, not a string operation over the raw text.

contradictions.sentence_a: When a change performs a cryptographic operation (encryption, password hashing, signing, generation of a non-guessable token) or sanitizes untrusted HTML, an established, maintained library or framework feature performs it (... for the HTML sanitization a well-known and secure sanitizer), and the change's own code supplies the inputs and consumes the result. (INP-11 Thesis; its bad half has `let clean = comment.replace("<script>", "");`)
contradictions.sentence_b: A regular expression whose pattern is only literal text, anchored at the start of the input, at its end, at both or at neither, with no flag, and that tests equality, a prefix, a suffix or containment, or, unanchored, replaces every occurrence of one fixed string with another, is written with the string type's own operation for that job, taking as its arguments the literal text the pattern matches and, for a replacement, the literal text it inserts, with anchors and escapes removed. (INP-15 Thesis) Its good half is `String flat = text.replace("--", "-");`, so its fix for `comment.replaceAll("<script>", "")` is `comment.replace("<script>", "")`, INP-11's bad line.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A replacement that removes markup or other dangerous text from untrusted input to sanitize it is outside the rule: its fix is a maintained sanitizer, not the string type's replacement.

contradictions.sentence_a: A regular expression whose pattern is only literal text, anchored at the start of the input, at its end, at both or at neither, with no flag, and that tests equality, a prefix, a suffix or containment, or, unanchored, replaces every occurrence of one fixed string with another, is written with the string type's own operation for that job, taking as its arguments the literal text the pattern matches and, for a replacement, the literal text it inserts, with anchors and escapes removed. (INP-15 Thesis) INP-17's good line `/^www\.example\.com$/.test(s)` is such a pattern anchored at both ends (JavaScript `$` without a flag matches only at the end of input), and INP-15's fix for INP-17's bad line `/www\.example\.com/.test(s)` is the containment `s.includes("www.example.com")`.
contradictions.sentence_b: A regular expression that decides whether a whole value has a format matches the entire value. It runs through the engine's full-match call where one exists, or it carries a start anchor and an end anchor with every alternative between them (INP-17 Thesis); A pattern without anchors accepts substrings that match it, which produces a partial comparison with the target, and untrusted input can bypass such a check by embedding one of the allowed patterns in an unexpected location. (INP-17 Rationale)
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A literal pattern that decides whether a whole value has a format, rather than finding text inside a larger text, becomes the string type's equality on the whole value, never a containment, prefix or suffix test, which would keep the partial match that lets a value embedding the literal pass.

contradictions.sentence_a: ... for the cryptographic operation an industry-validated implementation, called through the highest-level API it offers for the task, the one that handles IVs and similar parameters itself ... (INP-11 Thesis); Where a library is called, check whether the change picks IVs, nonces, salts, padding or the mode itself while the library offers a higher-level call that picks them. (INP-11 Validator)
contradictions.sentence_b: A random number or string that is intended to be non-guessable, such as an encryption key, an IV, a session id, a CSRF token or a password reset token, is generated by the platform's cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator ... (INP-12 Thesis), with the fix 'for an IV or nonce used with an encryption key ... the length its algorithm or requirement sets' (INP-12 Finding output): an IV the change draws from the secure generator and hands to a low-level cipher call is INP-12's good shape and INP-11's bad one wherever the library offers a call that draws the IV itself. INP-12's Limits ('choosing that method is cryptographic design, which this rule does not reach') name the cryptographic-design specialty, not this case, and a DEFER_TO cannot settle it because the INP-11 → INP-12 entry proposed above runs the other way.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Where the cryptographic library offers a call that draws the IV or nonce itself, the fix for an IV or nonce from a predictable source is that call, not a draw from the secure generator in the code.

summary: Five same-line overlaps need DEFER_TO entries (INP-09→INP-03, INP-11→INP-03, INP-11→INP-12, INP-01→INP-21, INP-01→INP-04), and INP-15's string-operation fix lands on shapes INP-13, INP-11 and INP-17 call bad, as INP-12's secure-generator IV lands on INP-11's low-level assembly; each wants a Limits sentence. Eight row concepts have neither card nor pending entry, four of them (XXE hardening, secrets and PII in logs, generic error messages, where a secret lives at run time) dropped between topics that each left them to another. Every card's trigger set matches its own bad Example but INP-15's set is nested in INP-19's, and the facets misplace `review` on 18 cards whose Theses never touch the change's shape, size or description, mark INP-03 and INP-06 mechanical though their Validators trace origins, and give INP-06 and INP-18 a hunk scope their Validators exceed.
